title: The Lesson I Learned From Hagar in the Wilderness
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Hagar in the Wilderness
The God Who Sees You When Everyone Else Walks Away
There are moments in life when the wilderness is not a place on a map.
It is a season.
A phone that never rings.
A prayer that seems unanswered.
A relationship that shattered.
A mistake you cannot undo.
A betrayal you never expected.
A future that suddenly disappeared.
Most people know what it feels like to stand in a wilderness.
What many do not realize is that one of the most powerful stories of grace in Scripture begins with a woman who found herself there long before most of us ever understood what loneliness felt like.
Her name was Hagar.
And if we're honest, many of us have been Hagar.
Not because we lived her exact story.
But because we know what it feels like to be forgotten.
To be used.
To be rejected.
To be blamed for circumstances we never created.
To carry wounds that were handed to us by someone else's decisions.
The story begins in Genesis 16.
Abram and Sarai had received God's promise of a child, but years passed without fulfillment. Instead of waiting on God, Sarai devised her own solution.
She gave Hagar, her Egyptian servant, to Abram.
The result was exactly what happens whenever human striving attempts to accomplish what only God can fulfill.
Pain.
Conflict.
Brokenness.
Hagar conceived, tension exploded within the household, and eventually she fled into the wilderness.
What makes this moment so remarkable is not merely that Hagar ran.
It is who found her there.
Genesis 16:7 says:
"The angel of the LORD found her by a spring of water in the wilderness."
The text does not say Hagar found God.
It says God found Hagar.
That changes everything.
Because there are seasons when we are too wounded to seek Him.
Too exhausted to pray.
Too broken to lift our eyes.
Too disappointed to know what to say.
Yet God still comes looking.
The Hebrew word often translated "found" here carries the sense of encountering someone intentionally.
This was not accidental.
The God of Heaven sought out a forgotten servant girl sitting alone in the desert.
And perhaps that is what someone reading this needs to hear today.
You may feel invisible.
But Heaven has not lost sight of you.
Then comes one of the most beautiful moments in all of Scripture.
Genesis 16:13 records Hagar's response:
"אֵל רֳאִי" (El Roi)
"You are the God who sees me."
This is the only place in Scripture where a person gives God this specific name.
El Roi.
The God who sees.
Not the God who notices from a distance.
Not the God who glances occasionally.
The God who truly sees.
He sees the tears nobody knows about.
He sees the anxiety hidden behind your smile.
He sees the battles you never post online.
He sees the fears that keep you awake.
He sees the trauma you still carry.
He sees the disappointment you cannot explain.
And He sees you without turning away.
That is grace.
Most of us think God's attention is reserved for heroes.
For prophets.
For kings.
For apostles.
Yet the first person in Scripture to call God "El Roi" was an Egyptian servant girl who had nothing to offer.
No title.
No influence.
No platform.
No status.
Only pain.
And somehow God met her there.
Maybe because grace has never been about what we bring.
Maybe grace has always been about who He is.
The wilderness was not the end of Hagar's story.
It became the place where she discovered God's character.
Many of us spend our lives trying to escape wilderness seasons as quickly as possible.
Yet some lessons can only be learned there.
In comfort we learn gratitude.
In success we learn stewardship.
But in wilderness seasons we learn dependence.
We learn that God is enough when everything else is stripped away.
We learn that His presence can sustain us when circumstances cannot.
We learn that His promises remain true even when our emotions tell us otherwise.
Years later, Hagar would find herself in another wilderness.
This time with her son Ishmael.
Food gone.
Water gone.
Hope gone.
Genesis 21 paints a heartbreaking scene.
A mother convinced she is about to watch her child die.
She places him beneath a shrub and walks away because she cannot bear to witness it.
Then she lifts her voice and weeps.
Perhaps some readers know exactly what that feels like.
Not literally.
But emotionally.
When you've reached the end of yourself.
When solutions disappear.
When strength evaporates.
When all you have left are tears.
Yet once again God intervenes.
Genesis 21:17 says:
"God heard the voice of the boy."
The Hebrew word is שָׁמַע (shama).
To hear attentively.
To listen with intention.
To respond.
God was not ignoring Hagar.
He was listening all along.
Then He opened her eyes to a well that had been there.
Not created.
Already there.
She simply could not see it.
How many times has God already placed provision near us while fear blinded us to its presence?
How many blessings have stood beside us unnoticed because panic was louder than faith?
How many wells exist that we have not yet seen?
The wilderness often convinces us God has abandoned us.
The Gospel reveals the opposite.
The wilderness is frequently where God reveals Himself most clearly.
Centuries after Hagar sat in her wilderness, another figure would walk into one.
Jesus.
Before beginning His earthly ministry, Christ entered the wilderness.
He faced temptation.
Isolation.
Testing.
Suffering.
Yet unlike us, He never failed.
He became the perfect Savior for imperfect people.
He entered our wilderness so that we would never walk through ours alone.
At the cross, Jesus experienced the ultimate abandonment.
He cried:
"Ἠλί, Ἠλί, λιμὰ σαβαχθανί"
"Eli, Eli, lama sabachthani?"
"My God, My God, why have You forsaken Me?" (Matthew 27:46)
Christ endured what we deserved so that we could receive what we never earned.
Grace.
Forgiveness.
Adoption.
Redemption.
New life.
The story of Hagar is ultimately not about Hagar.
It points us toward Jesus.
The God who sees.
The God who hears.
The God who pursues.
The God who redeems.
The God who rewrites stories.
Maybe you feel forgotten today.
Maybe you are carrying a secret failure.
Maybe someone wounded you deeply.
Maybe your life looks nothing like you imagined.
Maybe your wilderness feels endless.
Hagar's story reminds us that the desert is not proof of God's absence.
Sometimes it becomes the evidence of His nearness.
The same God who found Hagar still finds people today.
The same God who heard Hagar still hears people today.
The same God who provided for Hagar still provides today.
And the same Savior who died and rose again still transforms lives today.
That is the heartbeat of the Gospel.
From brokenness to redemption.
From shame to forgiveness.
From wandering to restoration.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
If this message spoke to your heart, don't keep it to yourself.
Have you ever experienced a wilderness season where God met you unexpectedly?
Or comment, "I have seen El Roi," if God has carried you through a season you thought would destroy you.
You will also gain access to ongoing discipleship content while helping make future Gospel-centered resources possible.
One day you may discover that the place you thought God abandoned you was actually the place where He was closest the entire time.
